package.name: Net
package.description: Networking: IP and socket addresses, TCP listeners and streams, UDP sockets, and name resolution

modules.name: Address
modules.header:
Internet addresses and the socket addresses made of one and a port: reading them from text and writing them back.
IPv4 addresses are read in dotted-decimal form only, without the octal and hexadecimal forms some C libraries
accept, which are a frequent source of confusion. IPv6 addresses are read with `::` compression and an embedded
IPv4 tail, and written in the canonical form of RFC 5952, which writes an IPv4-mapped address with its IPv4 tail in
dotted-decimal form.

modules.name: Dns
modules.header:
A DNS client of this package's own: `Resolver` asks name servers for a host's IPv4 and IPv6 addresses over UDP,
with TCP for an answer too long for a datagram. It is how `Resolve` works on Linux, where the system's resolver
belongs to the C library and a static binary has none: the hosts file answers first, as `getaddrinfo` would have
it, then the servers in `/etc/resolv.conf`. What the C library adds on top — search domains, the name service
switch, caching daemons — is left out: a name is looked up as it is written.

modules.name: Native
modules.header:
Sockets as each system makes them, behind one set of operations on a word-sized handle.
A socket is a descriptor on the Unix systems and a `SOCKET` on Windows; both fit in a word, so nothing above this
module asks which. Addresses are encoded here into the `sockaddr` bytes the system reads: the BSD systems start them
with a length byte and a one-byte family, Linux and Windows with a two-byte family, and every system puts the port
in network order. Errors become `IoError`s with the system's own code kept beside the meaning.

modules.name: Poll
modules.header:
Waiting on many sockets at once: a `Poller` holds the sockets registered with it, each with the readiness wanted and
a token the caller chooses, and `Wait` reports the ones that are ready with their tokens.
It is level-triggered on every system: a socket is reported for as long as it is ready, not only when it becomes so,
so a caller that reads part of what is waiting is told again. Linux uses epoll, FreeBSD and macOS kqueue, and Windows
`WSAPoll`, which has no registrations of its own, so the poller keeps them and hands the whole list over each time.
The sockets are meant to be non-blocking: readiness says a call would not wait, and a non-blocking socket fails
with `WouldBlock` in the rare case that it would after all.

modules.name: Resolve
modules.header:
Finding the addresses of a host by name.
On FreeBSD, macOS and Windows the system's resolver does the work: `getaddrinfo` reads the hosts file and asks the
name servers the system is configured with, so names resolve the way every other program on the machine resolves
them. On Linux that resolver belongs to the C library, which a static binary does not have, so this package reads
the hosts file and asks the configured name servers itself. A host that is already a numeric address is read
directly, without asking anyone.

modules.name: Tcp
modules.header:
TCP: a listener that accepts connections, and the connected streams it and `Connect` give.
A stream is an ordinary `Io` reader and writer. Reading past what the peer sent, once it has closed its side, fails
with `EndOfStream`; writing after the peer has gone fails with `BrokenPipe` or `ConnectionReset` rather than ending
the process with a signal. Every socket is closed when its value is dropped.

modules.name: Udp
modules.header:
UDP: datagrams sent to and received from any address, or to and from one connected peer.
Each send is one datagram and each receive takes one whole datagram; a datagram longer than the receive buffer is
cut to fit and the rest is lost, as the systems do. Nothing is resent or ordered.

doc.summary: Asks name servers for a host's addresses.
doc.markdown:
Asks name servers for a host's addresses. Not copied.
A query goes to each server in turn, for the IPv4 addresses and then the IPv6 ones, until a server answers;
the whole round is tried again as many times as the attempts allow. Each query waits for its answer up to the
timeout, and a name the server says does not exist ends the lookup at once.
